danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Netop på dette tidspunkt, under omstændigheder der var endnu vigtigere end at trække sig tilbage uden kamp, nemlig evakueringen og afbrændingen af Moskva, handlede Rostoptjin, der normalt fremstilles som ophavsmanden til den begivenhed, på en helt anden måde end Kutuzov.
Efter slaget ved Borodino var opgivelsen og afbrændingen af Moskva lige så uundgåelig som hærens tilbagetrækning bag Moskva uden kamp.
Enhver russer kunne have forudsagt det, ikke ved ræsonnement, men ved den følelse, der er indplantet i enhver af os og i vores fædre.

Det samme, der fandt sted i Moskva, var sket i alle byer og landsbyer på russisk jord fra og med Smolensk, uden grev Rostoptjins eller hans opslags medvirken. Befolkningen ventede fjenden uanfægtet, gjorde ikke oprør, blev ikke ophidsede og sled ikke nogen i stykker, men tog roligt imod sin skæbne, idet den følte i sig styrken til at finde, hvad den burde gøre i dette sværeste øjeblik. Og så snart fjenden rykkede nærmere, drog de velstående bort og efterlod deres ejendom, mens de fattigere blev og brændte og ødelagde det, der var tilbage.

Bevidstheden om, at det ville være sådan, og at det altid ville være sådan, var og er til stede i enhver russers hjerte. Og en bevidsthed om dette, og en anelse om at Moskva ville blive taget, var til stede i det moskvaanske samfund i 1812. De, der allerede havde forladt Moskva i juli og begyndelsen af august, viste, at de forventede dette. De, der rejste bort og tog med sig, hvad de kunne, og opgav deres huse og halvdelen af deres ejendele, gjorde det ud fra den latente patriotisme, der ikke udtrykker sig i fraser eller ved at ofre sine børn for at redde fædrelandet og lignende unaturlige heltegerninger, men umærkeligt, simpelt og organisk, og derfor på den måde, der altid frembringer de mest kraftfulde resultater.

»Det er skammeligt at flygte fra faren; kun kujonerne flygter fra Moskva,« fik de at vide. I sine opslag indprentede Rostoptjin dem, at det var skammeligt at forlade Moskva. De skammede sig over at blive kaldt kujonere, skammede sig over at rejse, men rejste alligevel, for de vidste, at det måtte gøres. Hvorfor rejste de? Det er umuligt at antage, at Rostoptjin havde skræmt dem med sine beretninger om de rædsler, Napoleon havde begået i erobrede lande. De første til at rejse var de rige, dannede mennesker, der udmærket vidste, at Wien og Berlin var forblevet uskadt, og at beboerne under Napoleons besættelse havde tilbragt deres tid behageligt i selskab med de charmerende franskmænd, som russerne, og især de russiske damer, dengang var så glade for.

De rejste, fordi der for russere slet ikke kunne være noget spørgsmål om, hvorvidt tingene ville gå godt eller skidt under fransk herredømme i Moskva. Det var utænkeligt at leve under fransk styre — det ville være det værste, der kunne ske. De rejste allerede inden slaget ved Borodino og endnu hurtigere derefter, på trods af Rostoptjins opfordringer til at forsvare Moskva eller hans bekendtgørelse om, at han agtede at tage det undergørende ikon af den Iberiske Gudsmoders med sig i kamp, eller om ballonerne, der skulle ødelægge franskmændene, og på trods af alt det vrøvl, Rostoptjin skrev i sine opslag. De vidste, at det var hærens sag at kæmpe, og at hvis den ikke kunne vinde, nyttede det ikke at tage unge damer og husfolk med til Tre Bakker-kvarteret i Moskva for at kæmpe mod Napoleon, og at de måtte rejse, hvor ked af det de end var over at overlade deres ejendom til ødelæggelse. De rejste uden at tænke på den uhyre betydning af, at den vældige og velstående by blev overladt til ødelæggelse, for en stor by med bygninger af træ ville med sikkerhed brænde ned, når den blev forladt af sine beboere. De rejste hver for sig, og dog var det netop på grund af deres afrejse, at den skelsættende begivenhed blev fuldbyrdet, som for altid vil forblive det russiske folks største ære. Damen, som af frygt for at blive standset af grev Rostoptjins ordrer allerede i juni var rejst med sine tjenere og sine hofnarre fra Moskva til sit gods i Saratov, med en vag fornemmelse af, at hun ikke var Bonapartes tjenerinde, udførte virkelig, simpelt og oprigtigt det store værk, der reddede Rusland. Men grev Rostoptjin, der snart hånede dem, der forlod Moskva, snart fik regeringskontorerne fjernet; snart uddelte helt ubrugelige våben til det berusede pøbelpak; snart lod processioner med ikoner afholde og snart forbød fader Augustin at fjerne ikoner eller helgenrelikvier; snart beslaglagde alle private vogne i Moskva og fjernede på hundrede og seksogtredive af dem den ballon, Lepnitj var ved at bygge; snart antydede, at han ville brænde Moskva og fortalte, hvordan han havde sat ild til sit eget hus; snart skrev en proklamation til franskmændene og bebrejdede dem højtideligt, at de havde ødelagt hans Børnehjem; snart krævede æren for at have antydet, at han ville brænde Moskva, og snart frasagde sig gerningen; snart befalede befolkningen at fange alle spioner og bringe dem til ham, og snart bebrejdede dem, at de gjorde det; snart udviste alle franske beboere fra Moskva og snart tillod Madame Aubert-Chalmé (midtpunktet for hele den franske koloni i Moskva) at blive, men beordrede den ærværdige gamle postmester Kljutjarev arresteret og forvist uden nogen særlig grund; snart samlede befolkningen ved Tre Bakker for at kæmpe mod franskmændene, og snart, for at slippe af med dem, udleverede han en mand til dem, der skulle dræbes, og kørte selv væk ad en bagport; snart erklærede, at han ikke ville overleve Moskvas fald, og snart skrev franske vers i stambøger om sin andel i sagen — denne mand forstod ikke meningen med det, der skete, men ville blot selv gøre noget, der ville forbløffe folk, udføre en patriotisk heltedåd; og som et barn legede han med den skelsættende og uundgåelige begivenhed — opgivelsen og afbrændingen af Moskva — og forsøgte med sin lille hånd snart at fremskynde, snart at standse den uhyre folkebølge, der bar ham med sig.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: At that very time, in circumstances even more significant than retreating without a battle — namely, the evacuation and burning of Moscow — Rostopchin, usually portrayed as the instigator of that event, acted in an entirely different manner from Kutuzov.
After the Battle of Borodino, the abandonment and burning of Moscow was as inevitable as the army's retreat beyond Moscow without fighting.
Every Russian could have predicted it — not through reasoning, but through the instinct planted in each of us and in our forebears.

The same thing that happened in Moscow had happened in every town and village on Russian soil from Smolensk onward, without any involvement from Count Rostopchin and his broadsheets. The people awaited the enemy calmly, without rioting or tearing anyone apart, but faced their fate with the inner strength to know what needed to be done at the most difficult moment. And as soon as the enemy drew near, the wealthy departed, abandoning their property, while the poor remained and burned and destroyed what was left.

The awareness that this would happen — that it would always happen — was and is present in the heart of every Russian. This awareness, this premonition that Moscow would be taken, existed in Moscow society in 1812. Those who had left the city already in July and early August showed they expected it. Those who departed, taking what they could and abandoning their homes and half their possessions, did so from a latent patriotism that expresses itself not through speeches or through giving up one's children to save the fatherland and similar unnatural gestures, but quietly, simply, organically — and therefore in the way that always produces the most powerful results.

"It is disgraceful to run from danger; only cowards are fleeing Moscow," they were told. In his broadsheets Rostopchin shamed them for leaving, insisting it was a disgrace. They were ashamed to be called cowards, ashamed to go — but they left anyway, knowing it had to be done. Why did they go? One can hardly suppose Rostopchin's horror stories about what Napoleon had done in conquered countries frightened them. The first to leave were the rich and educated, who knew perfectly well that Vienna and Berlin had remained intact, and that during Napoleon's occupation the residents had spent their time pleasantly in the company of charming Frenchmen, whom Russian women in particular found so appealing.

They left because for Russians there could be no question of whether things would go well or badly under French rule in Moscow. Being subject to French rule was out of the question — it would be the worst possible outcome. They left even before the Battle of Borodino, and even faster after it, despite Rostopchin's calls to defend Moscow, his announcement that he'd take the wonder-working icon of the Iberian Mother of God into battle, and his plans for hot-air balloons to destroy the French, and all the other nonsense he published in his broadsheets. They knew it was the army's job to fight, and if the army couldn't succeed, it made no sense to send young ladies and household servants to the Three Hills to fight Napoleon — they needed to leave, however sorry they were to abandon their property. They left without dwelling on the tremendous significance of a great city being handed over to destruction — for a great city of wooden buildings, once abandoned by its inhabitants, was certain to burn. Each left on his own account, and yet only because of their leaving was the momentous event accomplished that will always remain the greatest glory of the Russian people. The lady who, fearing she'd be stopped by Rostopchin's orders, had already moved to her Saratov estate in June with her household, with a vague sense that she was not Bonaparte's servant, was truly carrying out the great work that saved Russia. But Count Rostopchin — who now taunted those leaving, now had government offices evacuated; now distributed useless weapons to drunken mobs, now organized icon processions, now forbade Father Augustin to remove icons or holy relics; now seized all private carts in Moscow and used one hundred thirty-six of them to transport Leppich's balloon; now hinted he would burn Moscow and described setting fire to his own house; now published a proclamation solemnly scolding the French for destroying his orphanage; now claimed credit for suggesting Moscow be burned and now denied it; now ordered people to catch all spies and bring them to him, now reproached them for doing so; now expelled all French residents from Moscow, now let Madame Aubert-Chalme (the center of the entire French colony in Moscow) remain, while having the venerable old postmaster Klyucharev arrested and exiled for no particular offense; now assembled the people at the Three Hills to fight the French, and now, to be rid of them, handed over a man to be killed and himself slipped away by the back gate; now declared he would not survive Moscow's fall, now wrote French verses in albums about his role in the affair — this man did not understand the meaning of what was happening. He merely wanted to do something dramatic himself, to perform some patriotically heroic feat; and like a child he played games with the momentous, unavoidable event — the abandonment and burning of Moscow — and with his feeble hand tried now to speed, now to slow the enormous popular tide that carried him along.
